blocks.text: Different treatment methods are used depending on the type and severity of pollution, such as organic matter, chemicals or pathogens. They are used at different levels of treatment: primary treatment (removal of physical debris), secondary treatment (biological processing) and tertiary treatment (chemical purification). The main steps are as follows.

items: Screening and sedimentation: large insoluble particles are removed by passing the water through metal screens. In sedimentation the water is held in large tanks so that suspended solids settle to the bottom under gravity.

Coagulation and flocculation: to speed up the settling of fine colloidal particles, a chemical coagulant such as aluminium sulphate, Al2(SO4)3, is added when needed; dissolved contaminants (such as heavy metals and phosphates) are also precipitated in insoluble forms. The small particles clump together into larger masses called floc, which are easily removed.

Filtration: the water then passes through layers of graded sand and gravel, a mechanical process that removes the remaining fine suspended matter and some microorganisms; the sand traps particles in the pores between its grains. Activated carbon is used for more advanced purification.

Disinfection: filtration cannot remove dissolved ions or microscopic pathogens, so chemical treatment is needed. Chlorination is the most common method; others use sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl), ozone (O3) or sometimes hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Chlorine or sodium hypochlorite forms hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in water, which gets into bacteria and viruses and disrupts their cell functions.

Reverse osmosis (RO) and ion exchange: for high-purity water, such as for laboratories, or in very salty regions. RO uses a semi-permeable membrane that, under pressure, lets water through but holds back dissolved salts, bacteria and other impurities. Ion exchange is used to 'soften' water: hard water contains high concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions, which interfere with industrial processes and soap, and in an ion-exchange column these ions are swapped for Na+ or H+ ions.

blocks.alt: Three beakers of water. Before: white impurity particles are spread through the water. Coagulant added: a small yellow coagulant particle sticks to each impurity. Flocs settle: the particles have clumped together into flocs lying on the bottom. An arrow across the top reads: add a coagulant such as aluminium sulphate.
blocks.caption: Coagulation and flocculation (original diagram after the book's coagulation figure).
blocks.long_description: Fine particles are too small to settle on their own. The coagulant makes them stick together into heavier flocs, which sink and can be removed.

blocks.alt: Six tanks in a row joined by arrows, from waste water on the left to treated water on the right: screening (vertical bars), coagulation (chemicals added from above), flocculation (two paddles), sedimentation (sludge collecting at the bottom and removed), filtration (layers of sand over gravel) and disinfection (Cl2, NaOCl or O3 added). Notes below explain each step and give Cl2 + H2O -> HOCl + HCl.
blocks.caption: A water treatment plant (original diagram after Figure 33.4).
blocks.long_description: Each stage removes smaller impurities than the one before it: large objects, then settled solids, then floc, then fine particles, and finally microorganisms.

blocks.alt: Left: a tank divided by a dashed semi-permeable membrane; a piston applies pressure on the salty water side and an arrow shows water passing to the pure water side while orange salt particles stay behind. Right: an ion-exchange column packed with resin beads carrying Na+; hard water containing Ca2+ and Mg2+ enters at the top and soft water leaves at the bottom, with the equation 2RNa + Ca2+ -> R2Ca + 2Na+.
blocks.caption: Reverse osmosis and ion exchange (original diagram for topic 33.6).
blocks.long_description: Reverse osmosis pushes water against its natural direction of flow through a membrane that holds back salts. Ion exchange does not remove ions altogether; it swaps the hardness ions Ca2+ and Mg2+ for Na+ ions.

blocks.prompt: What is the chemical role of aluminium sulphate in water treatment?
blocks.explanation: It is a coagulant: it makes fine colloidal particles clump together into floc, which settles and is removed.

blocks.prompt: Why is boiling or filtration alone not enough to make polluted water safe?
blocks.explanation: Boiling kills most microorganisms but does not remove dissolved chemicals such as heavy metals; filtration removes suspended matter but not dissolved ions or all pathogens, so disinfection (and, if needed, RO or ion exchange) is also used.

items: Screening, sedimentation, coagulation and flocculation (Al2(SO4)3), filtration, disinfection (Cl2, NaOCl, O3: HOCl).
RO: membrane under pressure; ion exchange: Ca2+, Mg2+ swapped for Na+ or H+.
